meta.titre: Mass and weight: W = mg on Earth and on other planets

sections.contenu_markdown: A trader at Mile 12 market in Douala weighs tomatoes on a scale marked in kilograms, yet the word 'weight' in the physics class means something different. On the Moon an astronaut can jump much higher than on the Earth, although his body is made of the same amount of matter. The GCE often asks for the difference between mass and weight, and for a calculation with $W = mg$ on the Earth or on another planet. This is an easy topic to score on, if you keep the two quantities clearly apart.

items: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg) and the SI unit of force is the newton (N).
The Earth attracts every object towards its centre.

sections.titre: Mass, weight and the formula W = mg
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Mass** is the quantity of matter in a body. It is measured in kilograms (kg) with a beam balance or lever balance, which compares the body with standard masses. Mass is a scalar and it **does not change** from place to place. Mass is also a measure of inertia.

**Weight** is the force with which a planet pulls a body towards its centre. It is measured in newtons (N) with a spring balance (newton-meter). Weight is a vector, directed vertically downward, and it **changes** with the gravitational field strength $g$ at the place.

$$W = mg$$

where $W$ is the weight in newtons, $m$ is the mass in kilograms and $g$ is the gravitational field strength in $\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$.

| | Mass | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | amount of matter | pull of gravity on the body |
| Unit | kilogram (kg) | newton (N) |
| Type | scalar | vector (points downward) |
| Changes with place? | no | yes, it depends on $g$ |
| Measured with | beam or lever balance | spring balance |

Typical values of $g$: Earth $10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$, Moon about $1.6\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$. In deep space, far from any planet, $g$ is almost zero and weight is almost zero, but mass is unchanged.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When an object is moved to the Moon or another planet with a given $g$.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The mass stays the same. Find the weight with the new $g$: $W = mg_{\text{planet}}$. If the weight on Earth is given, first find the mass with $m = \dfrac{W}{10}$, then use the new $g$. To compare, $\dfrac{W_{\text{planet}}}{W_{\text{Earth}}} = \dfrac{g_{\text{planet}}}{g_{\text{Earth}}}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question moves a balance to another planet.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A beam balance compares the body with standard masses; both are pulled equally by gravity, so the balance reads the **same mass** anywhere. A spring balance measures the pull directly, so its reading changes with $g$. A spring balance marked in kilograms is only correct on the Earth.

sections.enonce_markdown: A sack of rice weighs $450\ \mathrm{N}$ on the Earth. (a) Find its mass. (b) Find its weight on a planet where $g = 4\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$. (c) What is its mass on that planet? Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ on the Earth.

etapes.action: Write the formula and make $m$ the subject.
etapes.justification: The weight is known and $g$ on the Earth is known, so the mass can be found.
Use the weight in newtons and $g$ in $\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ to give a mass in kilograms.

etapes.action: Find the weight on the planet.
etapes.justification: The mass is unchanged, but $g$ is now $4\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$.

etapes.action: State the mass on the planet.
etapes.justification: Mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on place.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The sack has a mass of $45\ \mathrm{kg}$ everywhere. Its weight is $450\ \mathrm{N}$ on the Earth and $180\ \mathrm{N}$ on the other planet.

items.pourquoi_faux: Weight is a force and is measured in newtons, while kilograms measure mass.

items.erreur_markdown: "On the Moon my mass is less because I am lighter."
items.pourquoi_faux: Mass does not change with place. Only the weight changes, because $g$ is smaller on the Moon.
items.correction_markdown: Mass is the same; weight on the Moon is about one sixth of the weight on the Earth.

items.pourquoi_faux: The formula is $W = mg$. Dividing gives a wrong unit and a wrong answer.

items.erreur_markdown: "A beam balance will give a smaller reading on the Moon."
items.pourquoi_faux: A beam balance compares masses, and both sides are pulled with the same $g$. It reads the same mass on the Moon.
items.correction_markdown: Only a spring balance reading would change.

items.erreur_markdown: "A body in space is weightless, so its mass is zero."
items.pourquoi_faux: Far from planets, weight is almost zero but the body still contains matter. Its mass has not changed.
items.correction_markdown: Mass stays the same; the weight depends on $g$.

items.enonce_markdown: Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$. (a) Find the weight of a bag of mass $2.5\ \mathrm{kg}$. (b) Find the mass of a pot whose weight is $140\ \mathrm{N}$.

A block hangs from a spring balance marked in newtons and reads $36\ \mathrm{N}$ on the Earth ($g = 10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$). On another planet the same balance reads $90\ \mathrm{N}$. (a) Find the mass of the block. (b) Find the value of $g$ on the planet. (c) What would a beam balance show there, using standard masses?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $m = \dfrac{36}{10} = \mathbf{3.6\ kg}$.

(b) $g = \dfrac{W}{m} = \dfrac{90}{3.6} = \mathbf{25\ N\,kg^{-1}}$.

(c) A beam balance compares masses, so it balances against standard masses totalling **$3.6\ \mathrm{kg}$**, the same as on the Earth.

items.enonce_markdown: A bridge sign says that the greatest weight it can safely carry is $55\,000\ \mathrm{N}$. An empty lorry has a mass of $3\,500\ \mathrm{kg}$ and is loaded with $40$ sacks of cocoa, each of mass $60\ \mathrm{kg}$. Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$. (a) Find the total mass and total weight. (b) Is the lorry allowed to cross? (c) What is the greatest number of sacks it can carry across?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Cocoa: $40 \times 60 = 2\,400\ \mathrm{kg}$. Total mass $= 3\,500 + 2\,400 = \mathbf{5\,900\ kg}$. Total weight $= 5\,900 \times 10 = \mathbf{59\,000\ N}$.

(b) $59\,000\ \mathrm{N} > 55\,000\ \mathrm{N}$, so the lorry is **not allowed** to cross.

(c) The greatest total mass is $\dfrac{55\,000}{10} = 5\,500\ \mathrm{kg}$, so the cocoa can have a mass of $5\,500 - 3\,500 = 2\,000\ \mathrm{kg}$. Number of sacks $= \dfrac{2\,000}{60} = 33.3$, so the lorry can carry at most **33 sacks** (33 sacks give a weight of $54\,800\ \mathrm{N}$; 34 sacks give $55\,400\ \mathrm{N}$, which is too much).

items_markdown: Mass is the amount of matter in kilograms; it is a scalar and the same everywhere, found with a beam balance.
Weight is the pull of gravity on a body in newtons; it is a vector pointing down, changes with $g$ and is found with a spring balance.
$W = mg$ with $g = 10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ on the Earth and about $1.6\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ on the Moon.
When a body moves to another planet, keep the mass and change $g$ to find the new weight.
Never write weight in kilograms or mass in newtons; check the unit of every answer.
